judge_assessment.explanation: Every judge claim checks out against the artifacts. I re-derived all eleven machine results independently from worksheet.pdf: f(3)=4(3)-7=5; H(4)=40 and H(6)-H(2)=100-40=60 from the Graph B readings that verify.json id 2/3 encode as data {0:0, 2:40, 4:40, 6:100, 8:60}; g(-2)=4+10+2=16; 4x-7=21 gives x=7; Table A rises 12 per hour so C(x)=12x+10 and C(6)=82; 480-24t=0 gives t=20; 480-24t=300 gives t=7.5; V(9)=264; the corrected 5-hour rental is 12(5)+10=70; and T(8)=72 is the largest range value. The graph data, Table A, the tank rule and the ticket story are mutually consistent, and the five pages extract cleanly with no clipping, so 'visually confirmed exactly twelve problems' and 'all pages legible and unclipped' both hold. The judge is also right that items 11(b) and 12 are the two manual items and that both model responses apply the contextual restrictions correctly. Where I part company is the perfect instruction_following score. The prompt ends 'clearly label any genuinely open response for manual review', and problem 10 prints 'Explain in one sentence what the student's rule ignores, then give the correct cost' while verify.json id 10 carries a single eval entry (12*x + 10 at x=5 = 70) and no manual entry. The Quick Answers bank on answer_key.pdf page 1 accordingly prints '10. 70' with none of the em-dash marking that item 12 gets, so nothing in the delivered package tells a grader that half of problem 10 needs a human. A second, smaller gap: problem 6(b) prints 'Write a rule for C(x), then use it to find C(6)' and verify.json covers only the value 82. Nothing in the verification data ties the rule 12x+10 back to Table A's four rows, so the sheet's own central object goes unchecked (it is in fact correct: 22, 34, 46, 58 at x=1..4).

strengths_to_preserve: Graph B carries an explicit scoping sentence on page 1: 'Used only by Problems 2 and 3. No other problem on this sheet refers to it.' On an interleaved sheet where a shared figure sits pages away from most items, this removes exactly the ambiguity that makes students hunt for a picture that is not theirs.

The Graph B data was designed so that H(2)=40 and H(4)=40, and the answer key's problem 2 teaching note uses it: 'the drone is at the same height at t = 2 and t = 4. Two different inputs may share one output - that is allowed for a function. Two different outputs for one input would not be.' The figure is not decoration; it is the counterexample the definition needs.

Problem 11 is split correctly at the verification layer: id 11 carries an eval entry (9*n at n=8 = 72) for part (a) and a separate manual entry whose desc names part (b) precisely. That two-entry decomposition of one printed problem is the right pattern, and it is what problems 6 and 10 on this same sheet are missing.

Problem 12 asks the student to compare the drone graph, the tank rule and the kayak table on the SAME question (realistic domain and range) and then justify which representation made it easier - a synthesis item that can only be answered by having done the earlier nine, rather than a harder instance of the last skill.

root_causes.description: The verification plan is built one machine result per problem rather than one entry per printed response slot, so a problem whose prose asks for two products (an explanation plus a number, or a rule plus a value) is recorded as fully covered once the number verifies. Nothing in the gate chain compares the number of requested responses against the number of declared entries, so gate_log.txt reports the run green with manual flags while problem 10's explanation is neither verified nor flagged.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 10 prints 'Explain in one sentence what the student's rule ignores, then give the correct cost (in dollars) of a 5-hour rental.' verify.json id 10 is a single {type: eval, expr: 12*x + 10, at: {x: 5}, expected: 70} with a trap, and no manual entry.

answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '10. 70' and '11. 72' with no manual marker, while '12. -' correctly signals the manual item - so the bank cannot distinguish a partly-open item from a fully machine-checked one.

worksheet.pdf problem 6(b) prints 'Write a rule for C(x), then use it to find C(6)'; verify.json id 6 has a read_data entry for the rate 12 and an eval of 12*x + 10 at x=6, but no entry whose expected value is the rule itself and no check binding 12x+10 to the four Table A rows.

SKILL.md line 257 already states the rule ('Use manual for ... any explanation/reasoning answer'), and SKILL.md line 189 shows why it is not enforced: verification hard-fails only 'unless every problem id 1..N has at least one check'.

improvements.title: Declare a manual entry for problem 10's explanation slot and gate on open-response verbs generally
improvements.proposed_change: Add a gate that scans each worksheet problem region for open-response verbs and constructions (Explain, Describe, Say why, Justify, Name the error, Sketch, Mark, Plot, In your own words, in complete sentences) and fails the build when the matching problem id in verify.json has no entry of type manual. For curr-270 the fix is one added entry under id 10 whose desc names the requested explanation (that the student's rule C(x)=22x ignores the fixed 10 dollar launch fee and treats the first hour's total as the hourly rate). Then make render_quick_answers.py append a manual marker to any bank row whose id carries a manual entry alongside machine entries, so '10. 70' becomes '10. 70, -' rather than reading as fully checked.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture pairing a worksheet problem whose prose is 'Explain in one sentence what the student's rule ignores, then give the correct cost' with a verify.json whose only entry for that id is the eval 12*x + 10 at x=5 = 70 - curr-270's own data. The new gate must exit non-zero naming the unflagged explanation in problem 10. Adding a manual entry under the same id must make the fixture pass and must make the rendered bank row show the manual marker.
improvements.expected_impact: A grader receiving this packet learns that problem 10 needs reading, not just checking. Across the run this is the second most common defect and it directly answers a clause the prompt states verbatim, so it lifts instruction_following on every case where an explanation currently hides inside an eval-only item.
improvements.risk: Verb matching over LaTeX prose will produce false positives on directions text and on answer-key language, so the scan must be restricted to worksheet problem regions with comments stripped, and needs an explicit opt-out marker for a problem where the verb appears in a quoted student claim rather than in an instruction to the reader.

improvements.title: Verify the rule a student is asked to write, not only the value computed from it
improvements.proposed_change: Build a response-slot inventory per problem from the worksheet source (each lettered sub-part and each conjoined request inside one sub-part counts as a slot) and require every slot to bind to a verify entry or an explicit manual entry. For a 'write a rule from this table' slot, the entry should be a check that the proposed rule reproduces every row of the source data - e.g. a read_data or eval entry per table row against 12*x + 10 - so the printed rule is verified against the givens rather than assumed. Fail the build when a slot count exceeds the bound entry count.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: worksheet problem 6 as printed (two lettered parts, part (b) asking for a rule AND C(6)) with curr-270's verify.json id-6 pair. The slot-coverage gate must exit non-zero naming the unbound rule slot in 6(b). After adding four eval entries binding 12*x + 10 to Table A's rows (22, 34, 46, 58 at x = 1, 2, 3, 4) plus the existing C(6) entry, the same fixture must pass.
improvements.expected_impact: Closes the run's dominant defect class. On this case it converts the sheet's central object - the rule built from Table A, which problems 6 and 10 both depend on - from an author assertion into a checked result, and it would have caught a mis-derived intercept before printing.
improvements.risk: Slot inventories built from prose will over-split some sentences, and forcing a machine check where only a manual one is possible would push authors to declare weak checks. The gate must accept a manual binding as satisfying a slot, and the reference material needs worked examples of when a slot is genuinely open.

case_summary: A strong interleaved Algebra 1 function-notation set that earned its ACCEPT: I re-derived all eleven machine results independently (5, 40, 60, 16, 7, rate 12 with C(6)=82, 20, 7.5, 264, 70, 72) and found no mathematical error, the Graph B readings and Table A rows are internally consistent, the answer key reasons rather than asserts, and the two-page study guide teaches the four faces of a function with a rule box, a worked example and a distinct try-it in each of its four sections. Two verification-coverage gaps survive the perfect score. Problem 10 asks for a written diagnosis before its number and is recorded as a bare eval, so the prompt's explicit instruction to label open responses is only partly met and the Quick Answers row '10. 70' looks fully checked. Problem 6(b) asks the student to write the rule C(x)=12x+10 and only the value 82 is verified, leaving the sheet's central object bound to Table A by assertion. Both are instances of the run's two dominant systemic findings, not case-specific slips, and neither changes the verdict.
